rv.q: He’s the beating heart of this restless, revealing production.
The added racial charge aside, this fittingly intense, non-conformist production delivers a chilling reminder of the perennial cost of dissent.
The show is a full-on onslaught with little modulation, compelling but exhausting.
Although Clint Dyer’s stirring take on Ken Kesey’s 1962 novel boldly reframes the story, the text can’t support his ideas.
But the bottom line is: it just doesn’t work.
Dyer has created something fresh and provoking.
Is it a rallying call to individuality and the exercising of free will to speak up and challenge those in authority?
That said, when he returns to the soil ruthlessly grabbed by genocidal invaders, it’s hard not to cheer.
One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest falls firmly in the first category.

cn.t: Dyer's bold reimagining with a predominantly Black cast offers a powerful lens on systemic oppression, anchored by Pierre's mighty performance as McMurphy, though critics debate whether the original text fully supports this provocative reframing.
